<div class="cp-header">
  <div class="cp-tag">Working Paper · 2025–2026</div>
  <h1 class="cp-title">
    Hazard or Amenity? Flood Risk, Waterway Proximity, and Uneven Housing Market Effects in Pierce County
  </h1>
  <div class="cp-meta">
    <span class="cp-author">Shuai Ma</span>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="cp-body">
  <h2 class="cp-section-heading">Abstract</h2>
  <div class="cp-abstract">
    <p>A home exposed to flooding is expected to sell at a discount. In Pierce County, Washington, however, I find no such discount. I argue that this missing discount is spatial in origin. Flood hazard and waterfront amenity are entangled on the same parcels, so an average flood-risk coefficient blends opposing capitalization pressures across sharply different market contexts, masking heterogeneity rather than measuring a uniform hazard penalty. The county's riverine floodplains and Puget Sound shoreline make this entanglement unusually measurable, and I trace its consequences through 47,763 arm's-length single-family sales from 2021 to 2025, linked to parcel, environmental, and neighborhood records. The overlap itself is nearly complete: parcels under Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) high-flood-risk designation are few, overwhelmingly water-adjacent, larger in lot size, and split between higher- and lower-income tracts. Hedonic regressions show what this bundling does to the price signal. Structural and neighborhood characteristics explain most of the variation in price; waterway proximity adds a premium of only about half a percent per halving of distance; and flood designation carries no discount, if anything a modest premium that weakens once floodplain distance is controlled. A flood–income–waterway typology traces the missing discount to heterogeneity within the designation, which covers affluent shoreline parcels where hazard travels with amenity as well as lower-income parcels where exposure compounds disadvantage. Machine-learning checks indicate that this pattern is not driven by functional form. Where hazard and amenity are spatially entangled, prices alone cannot reveal who bears flood risk and who profits from location; flood maps identify physical exposure, but not the distribution of market advantage or social vulnerability.</p>
  </div>
</div>
